subject: literature
passage: Many traditional ballads, especially those sung in rural communities, include a refrain, a line or two that returns after every verse. Because listeners often join in on such lines, refrains are usually explained as invitations for an audience to take part in the song. Folklorist Ilse Brandt, who studied recordings of ballad singers made in the early twentieth century, proposes a different primary function: refrains, she argues, gave singers a brief, familiar resting point in which to recall the next verse of a long story.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt's proposal?

choices.A: Some refrains in the recorded ballads consist of nonsense syllables with no clear meaning.
choices.B: When singers in the recordings faltered over a verse, they most often recovered right after a refrain.
choices.C: Many of the ballads in the recordings had also been printed on cheap song sheets sold at fairs.
choices.D: In recordings made at village gatherings, listeners can often be heard singing along with the refrains.

explanation.why: Brandt claims refrains mainly helped singers remember what came next. The most direct support would show refrains actually working that way during performance. Singers regaining their place just after a refrain shows the refrain giving them time to recall the next verse.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The meaning of a refrain's words does not show whether refrains helped singers recall verses.
explanation.B: Correct. Recovering right after a refrain suggests the refrain gave singers a pause in which to remember the next verse, as Brandt proposes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Whether ballads were also printed says nothing about what the refrains did for singers.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Listeners singing along fits the usual explanation, audience participation, rather than Brandt's memory explanation.
